source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas?
finding: Main claim: atypicality (A-index) and disruption (D-index) are negatively correlated. Atypical work extends ideas into new topics. Disruptive work replaces a dominant idea inside its own topic.
numbers: Corpus: 41M articles 1965-2024 (OpenAlex, 49M raw). Fig 3: 40,935,251 papers; mean D falls across A-index bins in every discipline, period and team-size stratum. No correlation coefficient is given in the text.
quote: Atypicality and Disruption Are Negatively Correlated
limits: Preprint. The text gives bin plots, no effect size and no controls table. The sign conflicts with the 2022 paper (see b05).
agent_relevance: Do not treat 'distant combination' and 'replace the leader' as one move. Open mode needs two separate attempt types.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas?
finding: Fig 2 trend: top-5% atypical papers rise over time while top-5% displacing papers fall.
numbers: 40,453,825 articles 1965-2020. Cut-offs: top 5% atypical A>22.9; top 5% displacing D>0.04.
limits: Cut-offs are percentile thresholds. The disruption decline is itself contested (b11 to b14).
agent_relevance: Wider recombination did not bring more displacement. A search that only widens will not replace the incumbent answer.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas?
finding: An LLM judged topical similarity between a paper and its most-cited reference. Highly disruptive papers are topically close to that reference. Highly atypical papers are far from it. This supports displacement, not recombination, as the route to disruption.
numbers: Strong topical correspondence for disruptive papers after controls for field, citation count and time. Exact coefficients are not in the text I read.
limits: The exact LLM and prompt for the similarity score are not stated in the text. Here the LLM is a measuring tool, not the object studied.
agent_relevance: A cheap code-side check exists: embed the new attempt and its closest rival, and tell displacement (near) from extension (far).

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas?
finding: Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct zero-shot labelled disruptive papers as 'theory' (conceptually different) or 'method' (refinement). Theory-type advances come soon after their reference; method-type ones later. Result survived few-shot prompts, reworded options and an 'others' option.
numbers: N=50,147 highly cited D>0 papers in the text (Fig 4 caption says 52,488 papers 1900-2020). Output was the token probability of 'theory'. Mean theory probability falls as the gap to the reference grows.
limits: One LLM family, no human gold labels reported. The probability is a model-confidence proxy. Hypothesis 2 (theories are harder to displace) rests on this labelling.
agent_relevance: LLM labelling of 'concept vs refinement' is a soft signal. It needs a human-checked sample before the agent relies on it.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) New directions in science emerge from disconnection and discord (J. Informetrics)
finding: The same group's earlier paper found the opposite direction: atypical papers more often disrupt. Highly atypical papers are nearly twice as likely to disrupt as conventional ones, but the D-score takes about 10 years to settle.
numbers: Highly novel vs conventional: 61% vs 36% disruptive. Typicality vs D: Pearson r=-0.05, p<0.001 (lower typicality, higher D; very weak). Only 2.3% of papers are highly atypical; the share fell from 3.9% (1970) to 1.4% (2000). 1970 cohort 87,475 papers. D reaches 80% of its final value in about 10 years.
quote: Atypical papers are nearly two times more likely to disrupt science than conventional papers
limits: Uses z-scores of journal pairs (low z means atypical), so the sign convention differs from the 2025 A-index. The correlation is tiny (|r|=0.05). Same lab, two papers, opposite headlines.
agent_relevance: This is the key unresolved conflict. Atypicality may help disruption in the long run yet predict topic extension. Test both in our own loop; trust neither sign.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022)
finding: Moderators: the effect is larger in 'artificial' fields (computer science, engineering) than in natural sciences. Citation impact peaks for papers mixing typical and atypical references, but the chance of disruption peaks for the highly atypical.
numbers: Top-5% disruptive vs top-5% developing papers differ in z-median distribution: KS D=0.14 (z-min D=0.09), p<0.001. High vs low impact: KS D=0.15. Late-year t-statistics for disruptive-citation fraction, novel vs conventional: 23.85 (1970), 33.04 (1980), 52.78 (1990), 88.76 (2000), with cohorts of 87k to 592k papers.
limits: Large t-values come from huge samples, not large effects. Cohorts start in 1970.
agent_relevance: A conventional base with a small atypical share wins on impact. A bold all-atypical bet wins on disruption but only slowly. This matches a split between safe selection and open mode.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact (Science), as summarised by Lin et al. 2022
finding: Founding result, known here only second-hand: papers that mix mostly conventional references with a small tail of atypical ones are the most likely to be highly cited. Lin et al. 2022 say they confirmed it in their data.
numbers: Uzzi's own numbers were not read this session.
limits: Original not opened. Do not cite its numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: A 'conventional base plus a small atypical share' mix is a ready design rule for open mode.

source: Leibel, Bornmann (2023) What do we know about the disruption index in scientometrics?
finding: Review of the validity of DI1 and its variants. Convergent-validity evidence is mixed; DI5 and some variants do better than DI1. Disruption and novelty are different constructs.
numbers: Leahey et al. 2023: new methods raise disruption, new theories and results lower it. Shibayama and Wang 2020 (246 survey responses, 546 papers): self-rated theoretical originality links to their score with r about 0.10 to 0.17; methodological originality does not.
quote: Although novelty may be necessary for disruptiveness, it is not necessarily sufficient
limits: The two novelty-type results conflict (method vs theory drives disruption). The review calls them inconclusive.
agent_relevance: Atypicality is not a clean predictor of disruption, and which TYPE of novelty matters is disputed.

source: Leibel, Bornmann (2023) review
finding: Nobel-prize validation of the disruption index does not replicate cleanly. Wu et al. 2019 found Nobel papers in the top 2%. Later studies found no difference or mixed signs.
numbers: Wu 2019: 877 Nobel papers, mean D=0.10, vs 3,372,570 controls. Wei 2020: 557 Nobel vs 557 matched papers, mean D 0.236 vs 0.239, p=0.898. S. Wang 2023 logistic DI1 coefficient -6.777, p=0.125. Wei 2023: DI1 coefficient 0.071, p<0.001.
limits: Samples, years, controls and index variants differ, so no clean pooling.
agent_relevance: If the 'breakthrough' metric is shaky, any reward built on it is shaky. Use it as a hint, not a score.

source: Leibel, Bornmann (2023) review
finding: Expert-label validity (Faculty Opinions tags) is split. DI5 and a variant (DEP) did best against 'new finding' tags. Against breakthrough-paper labels DI5 and DI1 gave breakthroughs lower scores than other papers; only MeSH-based variants pointed the right way. Reviewer ratings did not correlate with disruption scores in one study.
numbers: Table 5 reports 45 Poisson regressions. Reference-count effect is non-linear: negative below about 10 references, positive above 10 in five WoS fields, negligible in management and engineering (Ruan 2021).
limits: Reported second-hand through the review. Citation window and discipline change results.
agent_relevance: Different 'breakthrough' labellers disagree, so no single gold standard exists for a selection check.

source: Petersen, Arroyave, Pammolli (2023) The disruption index is biased by citation inflation
finding: Challenge to Park et al. 2023 (Nature). The CD index falls over time because reference lists grow and citation links densify, so the decline is a measurement artifact. Argued three ways: deduction, data, simulation.
numbers: Network links grow about 5% a year (rate 0.051); the citation total doubles every 13.6 years. Longer reference lists raise the chance that a reference is co-cited, which pushes CD toward 0.
limits: Preprint at this version. Rival work (b16) says the findings survive some of these checks.
agent_relevance: Any metric tied to counts drifts with corpus size. Scores in the loop must be normalised against the same pool.

source: Petersen, Arroyave, Pammolli (2024) The disruption index suffers from citation inflation and is confounded by shifts in scholarly citation practice
finding: Quasi-experiment: PNAS Plus (online-only, longer reference lists) vs PNAS. The difference in |CD| is explained entirely by reference-list length. In SciSciNet, disruption rose slightly 2005 to 2015. The team-size effect is tiny and turns positive at 8 or more authors.
numbers: 18,644 PNAS articles 2011-2015; 12.6% PNAS Plus. Coefficient on reference length b_r=-0.0039 (95% CI -0.0055 to -0.0023). 100% of the PNAS/PNAS Plus gap comes from reference count. About 35% decrease in CD from 20 years of network density. Regression sample 7,768,207 papers.
limits: Uses a fixed 5-year window. Lin et al. 2025 (b17) show window length reverses the team-size sign.
agent_relevance: Reference-list length is a hidden driver. Control how many sources an attempt cites before scoring its novelty or disruption.

source: Holst, Algaba, Tori, Wenmackers, Ginis (2024) Dataset Artefacts are the Hidden Drivers of the Declining Disruptiveness in Science
finding: Failed replication of the decline. A plotting bug hid papers with CD5=1, most of which have zero recorded references. Excluding them removes the decline in papers and reduces it in patents. Random rewiring also reproduces the decline.
numbers: 972,161 hidden papers and 142,362 hidden patents with CD5=1. In SciSciNet (39,888,199 papers) 97% of CD5=1 papers, and in PatentsView 78% of such patents, have zero references. R2 of the Park regression rises from 0.10 to 0.52 (patents) and 0.15 to 0.95 (papers) with a zero-reference dummy. In 100 sampled records, 93% of papers and 98% of patents do cite in the PDF.
limits: Lin et al. 2025 (b16) reply that the Holst data had about 3x more zero-reference records, and cite Park et al. 2025 as robust to excluding them. Not settled.
agent_relevance: Empty or degenerate inputs can drive a headline trend. The harness needs guards for empty attempts.

source: Bentley, Valverde, Borycz, Vidiella, Horne, Duran-Nebreda, O'Brien (2023) Is disruption decreasing, or is it accelerating?
finding: With a citation-weighted disruption index on the same dataset, disruption stays near its neutral value over fifty years and rises modestly since 2000. The fall in unique words is expected in an exponentially growing corpus.
numbers: Weighted index sits near zero (about -0.01 to -0.02 in the figure) since about 1970.
limits: Preprint. The weighting is the authors' own choice; it is another specification, not ground truth.
agent_relevance: Different weightings give different trend signs. Report a trend only when several specifications agree.

source: Leibel, Bornmann (2024) Specification uncertainty: what the disruption index tells us about the multiverse of bibliometric indicators
finding: Disruption scores involve many hidden analyst choices (citation window, thresholds, self-citation handling, variants). Defensible choices can give different results. The authors propose multiverse-style reporting.
numbers: No new effect size. Cites a many-analysts study (Schweinsberg 2021: 19 analysts, a broad range of results).
limits: Letter to the editor: argument, not a measured test.
agent_relevance: Run several scoring variants for any selection signal and act only when they agree.

source: Lin, Li, Wu (2025) The Disruption Index Measures Displacement Between a Paper and its Most Cited Reference
finding: The authors' reframing: D measures relative innovation, a paper's ability to displace its most-cited reference. Reference citations follow Zipf's law; the top reference gets about 40% of all reference citations. Expert nominations agree with D.
numbers: 20 scholars, 190 nominations: disruptive nominees mean D=0.21 (top 1%); consolidating nominees mean D=-0.011 (bottom 13%); AUC=0.83. Cmax/Ctotal 0.40 observed vs 0.42 predicted. 49,077 papers (over 100 cites, D>0.2): 0.52 chance of sharing a field with the top reference vs 0.014 at random, about 37x. Only 38% of 42M papers have D>0.
quote: D-index captures relative innovation: a paper's ability to displace its most-cited reference
limits: Authors defend their own index; the expert panel is small (20). Same group as the 2025 atypicality paper.
agent_relevance: Replacement needs a named incumbent. The selection step could require each new attempt to state which earlier attempt it supersedes.

source: Lin, Li, Wu (2025) Team Size and Its Negative Impact on the Disruption Index
finding: Boundary condition: window length flips the sign. With a 5-year window, large teams look more disruptive, as Petersen found. With longer windows the negative link returns, turning at about 10 years. Small teams act like sleeping beauties.
numbers: Reproduced Petersen's model on the same data: positive at 5 years. Windows tested: 25, 20, 10, 5, 3 and 1 year. Original study: 65M projects across papers, patents and software.
limits: Authors are the original authors of the finding.
agent_relevance: Slow-acting disruptive ideas look bad early. Scoring ideas too soon under-credits them.

source: Huang, Xie (2026) Large scientific teams are more, not less, disruptive
finding: A newer challenge: equalising reference counts reverses the team-size gradient. A one-reference-at-a-time measure separates recognised breakthroughs from ordinary papers better than standard D.
numbers: About 60M publications. AUC of the new measure 0.94 to 0.98 on six benchmarks. Standard D: Turing 0.79, Nobel 0.73, Lasker 0.60, Test of Time 0.55, Physical Review Milestones 0.40, Science Breakthrough of the Year 0.26 (below chance).
limits: Preprint (v2, Oct 2026), not peer reviewed here. Proposes its own measure.
agent_relevance: Standard D can rank recognised breakthroughs below random papers. Do not use it as a reward.

source: Larregue, Gingras (2026) The disruption index does not measure scientific innovation
finding: Critique of a 2026 Science paper (Cui et al.) that links disruption to career age. Country ranking by share of 'disruptive' articles puts Iraq and Nigeria at the top. They also argue that the shift in reference age predates the 1994 end of mandatory retirement.
numbers: Iraq 57.5% and Nigeria 56% of articles with a positive disruption index.
limits: Opinion plus re-analysis of one paper; the target paper was not read here.
agent_relevance: A metric that ranks small producers on top may be measuring small-sample noise.

source: Fang, Evans (2025) Generalization and the Rise of System-level Creativity in Science
finding: A third framework: foundation, extension and generalization indices from citation roles. Correlations between atypicality or surprise and these indices are modest, so how a paper is built differs from how it is later used.
numbers: Foundation index 0.059 (1950) to 0.025 (1990), -57.6%. Extension 0.536 to 0.762, +42.2%. Generalization 0.405 to 0.214, -47.2% over the same span.
limits: Preprint. Indices are the authors' own definitions.
agent_relevance: More evidence that input mix and later role are separate things.

source: Fang, Evans (2025)
finding: Quasi-experiment on LLM use: after authors first show detected LLM use, their references shift toward generalizing, cross-field works.
numbers: Stacked difference-in-differences: +0.050 SD (arXiv, 95% CI 0.030 to 0.071), +0.117 SD (bioRxiv, CI 0.060 to 0.174), +0.081 SD (SSRN, CI 0.005 to 0.157). 65,072 treated arXiv authors.
limits: LLM use is inferred by a detector, not observed; adopters self-select. The authors urge caution.
agent_relevance: A weak sign that LLM help pushes toward cross-field citing (the atypical side), not toward replacing leaders.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?
finding: Blind expert review: LLM ideas were rated more novel than expert human ideas, and slightly weaker on feasibility.
numbers: Novelty mean 4.84 human (N=49), 5.64 AI (N=49), 5.81 AI plus human rerank; p<0.05. 79 reviewers, 298 unique reviews, 49 idea writers.
limits: Novelty is a reviewer rating, not atypicality or disruption. Reviewer agreement was only 56.1% (NeurIPS 2021: 66.0%).
agent_relevance: LLMs make novel-looking ideas. This tests the recombination side only.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024)
finding: Limits of LLM ideation: low diversity and unreliable self-evaluation.
numbers: Of 4000 seed ideas only about 200 were non-duplicates (about 5%, cosine similarity cut 0.8). LLM judges reach at best 71.4% accuracy (Claude-3.5-Sonnet) on accepted vs rejected papers; 61.1% and 63.5% for two other models.
limits: Agent baseline built on Claude-3.5-Sonnet; NLP topics only.
agent_relevance: Repeated samples from one model collapse toward duplicates. This matches guardrail G4.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: Randomised execution test: 43 experts spent over 100 hours each executing LLM or human ideas. LLM ideas lost far more score after execution; the ideation-stage novelty lead vanished and for some metrics flipped.
numbers: Score change after execution: human ideas novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052; AI ideas -1.049, -1.760, -1.879 (1-10 scale), p<0.05 FDR corrected. After execution excitement 3.90 (AI) vs 4.48 (human) and effectiveness 4.13 vs 4.78 (not significant, N=43). Ideation-execution correlations weak; moderately negative for AI excitement.
quote: LLM-generated ideas decrease significantly more than expert-written ideas
limits: NLP prompting ideas only; 58 reviewers; the rank flip is not significant.
agent_relevance: Novelty-as-appearance does not survive execution. Use a real check (G2, G3) before trusting a novel attempt.

source: Cross-source synthesis
finding: What holds up: (1) atypicality and disruption are separate, weakly related measures; (2) the sign of their link depends on definition and window (2022: atypical papers more often disrupt; 2025: A-index and D negatively related); (3) the headline 'science is getting less disruptive' fails several robustness checks and the Nobel validation is mixed.
numbers: Replications and critiques: b11 to b15, b18, b19. Defenders: b16, b17.
limits: Both camps include authors of the original index, and many sources are preprints.
agent_relevance: Treat both metrics as noisy hints. Open mode should try both move types and check by outcome, not by a metric.

source: Cross-source synthesis
finding: No source found that directly tests LLM agents on the atypicality or disruption of their own outputs. Closest LLM work: ideation novelty ratings (Si 2024), the execution gap (Si 2025), the LLM-adopter citing shift (Fang 2025), and LLM as similarity or theory/method labeller (Li 2025).
numbers: 4 LLM-related groups in this file. Search was limited: arXiv and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate-limited; one WebSearch used.
limits: Absence of evidence in a limited search, not proof.
agent_relevance: Open question: measure whether the agent's attempts are near or far from the incumbent answer, then see which kind passes held-out checks.
